problem: Zero-shot ObjectNav agents model the decision-making side of search poorly. Learned policies (RL/IL from simulator rollouts) generalize badly to new scenes and objects. Explicit modular methods use only two hand-thresholded states (explore / identify), so they cannot exploit scene context or take extra views to verify a detected target, and they often stop on false-positive detections.
motivation: Visual foundation models have largely solved open-vocabulary perception, so the bottleneck has shifted to cognition, i.e. deciding what to do next. Neuroscience findings suggest humans keep and continually update fine-grained cognitive states during object search, such as using context or re-observing to verify. Learning transitions between such fine-grained states would need large amounts of demonstrations, so the paper lets a frozen LLM reason the transitions from a text-serialized map.
key_idea: A 5-state finite state machine models the ObjectNav cognitive process (Broad Search → Contextual Search → Observe Target → Candidate Verification → Target Confirmation). A frozen LLM chooses state transitions and state-specific landmark goals, prompted with landmark-centred text built from an online heterogeneous cognitive map (VLM-refined 3D scene graph + Voronoi landmark graph + occupancy map).
insight: The gains come mainly from success rate, not efficiency. Adding states monotonically raises SR on HM3D: BS+OT 55.2 → +CS 57.6 → +CV 67.2 / +TC 68.8 → all five 72.5 (Table 3). The Candidate Verification state is what lets the agent recover from misdetections such as a sofa misread as a bed. It costs path length: dropping CV lowers SR to 68.8 but raises SPL from 26.2 to 33.6. Prompt ablations (Table 4) show the grounding matters: using only object categories drops SR to 63.3, removing agent-to-landmark spatial info (distance/path) gives 64.5, removing navigation history 67.8, removing scene-graph edges 68.2, removing room type 71.6. So spatial/relational structure, rather than room labels, is what makes LLM reasoning useful. When CogNav uses the same state sets as L3MVN, SG-Nav or TriHelper, it still beats them, which the authors attribute to the cognitive-map prompt format.
method: Heterogeneous cognitive map C_t = {S_t, M_t, L_t}, built online from posed RGB-D (640×480, depth 0.5–5 m).

Scene graph S_t: OpenSEED open-vocab 2D segmentation is back-projected into a global voxel grid, and instances are fused ConceptGraphs-style with DBSCAN. Every 10 steps GPT-4V with Set-of-Mark images resolves ambiguous merges (over/under-segmentation), labels edges from {next to, on top of, inside of, under, hang on, none} (geometric ones computed directly), and assigns room types.
Occupancy map M_t: SemExp-style top-down 960×960 grid at 5 cm, with channels for obstacles, explored area, agent location and projected instances, updated every step.

Landmark graph L_t: frontiers are clustered (L3MVN) and a Generalized Voronoi Diagram is skeletonized from traversable area (VoroNav). It is reduced to intersections plus leaf nodes; each leaf is mapped to an object or frontier, nearby leaves are fused, and at least 2 leaves per object are kept to enable multi-view verification. Updated every 10 frames.

Cognitive map prompting: per landmark, map-to-landmark text (nearby objects with scene-graph relations, room type, frontier flag if within 1 m of a frontier) and agent-to-landmark text (direction, Dijkstra path and distance on the landmark graph, explored-before flag).

LLM state machine: the LLM (GPT-3 per the main text) is queried with the prompt to pick the next of 5 states (BS, CS, OT, CV, TC), then queried again to select a landmark from the state-specific candidate subset (frontier / target-relevant / target / unvisited-target landmarks). In TC the landmark nearest the target is chosen deterministically. Backward transitions such as CV → BS allow error recovery.
Low-level execution: the Fast Marching Method plans discrete actions to the chosen landmark. STOP is issued upon reaching the TC landmark, with a 500-step budget and 1 m success radius.

setting.backbone: GPT-3 (LLM, frozen; state transitions + landmark selection) + GPT-4V (VLM, frozen; scene-graph fusion, edges, room type) + OpenSEED (2D open-vocab detection/segmentation); ablations swap in Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and CogVLM2-llama3-chat-19B
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (640×480) + agent pose (x, y, θ)
setting.action_space: high-level: LLM-selected Voronoi landmark; low-level via FMM: MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN 30° / LOOK UP / LOOK DOWN / STOP
setting.privileged: none (uses simulator-provided agent pose, standard for modular ObjectNav)

numbers_note: HM3D episode count is ambiguous: the text says HM3D val has 2K episodes, but the failure analysis ('277/1008') suggests about 1008 episodes were evaluated, so HM3D entries are flagged as a probable subset. MP3D is described as 1.8K val episodes over 20 categories, which differs from the usual 2,195-episode / 21-category MP3D val. DTG is reported only for HM3D. Per-category results: HM3D in Table 2 (CogNav category-mean 71.3); MP3D per-category only in a supplementary figure without numbers. LLM naming is inconsistent: the main text says GPT-3 is the LLM, but supp. Table 3 lists 'Cognitive Process Modeling with GPT-4v'. The text claims removing CV raises SPL by 7.8, while Table 3 gives 26.2 → 33.6 (+7.4). Real-robot results are qualitative only.
results: Training-free CogNav sets a new zero-shot ObjectNav SR on all three benchmarks, a relative gain of at least 14%: HM3D 72.5 SR / 26.2 SPL vs TriHelper 62.0 / 25.3; MP3D 46.6 / 16.1 vs SG-Nav 40.2 / 16.0; RoboTHOR 54.6 / 24.3 vs SG-Nav 47.5 / 24.0. SPL gains are marginal, since verification adds path length. With fully open-source Llama3.1-8B + CogVLM2 it still reaches 62.6 SR on HM3D, matching TriHelper's 62.0.
limitations: Relies on the 2D foundation detector (OpenSEED). 35.7% of HM3D failures come from persistent detection failures, and 64.3% from target inaccessibility (mesh artifacts, stairs).

Path efficiency barely improves (SPL gains ≤0.9 over the best baseline) because candidate verification requires extra viewpoints. Inference is slow: multiple GPT-4V/LLM API calls, about 3.4 s per state-reasoning query and 1.8 s per scene-graph update.
Limited to object-goal navigation (no free-form instructions). It depends on closed commercial APIs (GPT-3/GPT-4V), with a sizeable drop when replaced by open models (72.5 → 62.6 SR).
